$2,300 per day in ad spend. 
Same bids at 2am and 2pm.
Conversion rate at 2am: 1.1%. 
Conversion rate at 2pm: 6.4%.

Every click cost the same. One hour returned profit. The other burned it.

At $2,300 a day, that gap isn't a rounding error. Run the math across a 30-day window and the dead hours alone account for $8,000–$12,000 in spend that converted at a fraction of the rate the account average suggested. Budget wasn't the problem. Distribution was.

Amazon doesn't adjust your bids by hour. The platform treats midnight and midday as identical. Most sellers spending $50,000+ per month never question that, because Campaign Manager doesn't surface hourly conversion data in any default view. You have to pull it manually.

Once you do, the pattern is immediate.

Conversion rate is not flat across 24 hours. For most products, a small cluster of hours carries a disproportionate share of profitable orders. The remaining hours still consume budget — same CPC, lower CVR, weaker return.

Day parting fixes the mismatch by adjusting bids to match the conversion curve.

→ Hours where CVR runs 30%+ above your daily average: increase bids. Concentrate budget where the return is strongest.
→ Hours where CVR drops 50%+ below average: reduce bids aggressively. At $2,300/day, every wasted hour costs real margin.
→ Hours sitting near average: hold. Review weekly — patterns shift with seasonality and competition.

Pull a 30-day hourly report from Campaign Manager. Calculate CVR per hour. Compare each hour to the daily average. Flag the zones. Adjust bids accordingly.

The whole process takes under 20 minutes with the right tracker.

A seller came to us last month. Spending $14K/mo on ads. ACOS looked fine. Keywords were solid.

But something didn't add up.

His CPC on top exact-match terms was 40-60% higher than the category average. No new competitors had entered. His bids hadn't changed. Nothing in the market explained it.

So we pulled his Search Term Report and sorted it across campaigns.
That's when we found it.

4 of his own campaigns were targeting the same keywords. In the same auctions. Bidding against each other. 

Amazon was treating his own ads like they were 4 different competitors — and charging him accordingly.

He'd been paying premium CPC against himself for months.

This is called internal cannibalization. It comes in 3 forms:

Exact overlap — same keyword in multiple campaigns. Both enter the auction. CPC rises on both.

Match type bleed — "running shoes" as broad in one campaign, exact in another. The broad match picks up the exact term. Now both compete for the same query with different bids.

ASIN-level — two of your own products target the same keyword. Amazon puts both in. One steals the other's clicks. Neither gets enough data to optimize.

Most sellers have no idea this is happening because Seller Central doesn't flag it.

Checking manually means downloading your STR, sorting it, and cross-referencing every keyword across every campaign. On big accounts, that's hours.

So we built a tool that does it in 2 minutes. Upload your report — Sponsored Products or Sponsored Brands — and it maps every conflict.

posts.text:
Most sellers look at their competitors once — when they launch.

They check the main image, note the price, read a few reviews. Then they move on.

That is not a competitive analysis. That is a glance.

A real competitor map covers four dimensions. Run it before any major decision: a price change, a listing update, a new variation, or a category entry.


THE COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK

Step 1 — Keyword Footprint

Use a tool like Helium 10 or Data Dive to pull the organic keyword rankings for your top 3 competitors.
→ Which keywords are they ranking for that you are not?
→ Which keywords are they ranking in positions 1–5 that you are outside the top 20?
→ That gap is your opportunity map — and your vulnerability if a competitor already owns it

Step 2 — Review Profile Breakdown

Do not just note their star rating. Go deeper.

→ Read their 1-star and 2-star reviews — these are a free product roadmap

→ What complaints repeat? That is a gap you can build your differentiation around 
→ What are they praised for? That is the minimum standard buyers expect in this category

Step 3 — Pricing and Offer Structure

Check their current price, historical price trend, and any active promotions.
→ Are they running coupons, bundles, or strike-through pricing permanently? 
→ A competitor with a consistent coupon is not really priced where the listing shows
→ Understanding true effective price tells you where the conversion floor actually sits

Step 4 — Listing Execution Quality

Score their listing against a simple rubric: main image, image suite, title structure, bullet point depth, and A+ content quality.
→ Is the A+ content converting or just decorating?
→ Are bullet points feature-led or benefit-led?
→ This tells you whether they are winning on product or on marketing — and which one you need to beat

Build this map before you make any significant decision about your own product.

Most Amazon mistakes happen because sellers are reacting to their own data without knowing where they actually stand in the category.

The competitor map tells you that.

Amazon sellers are leaving their best keyword data on the table.

Not because it's hard to find. Not because it requires expensive tools.


Because most sellers turn off the one campaign that generates it — right when it starts working.

Most sellers treat Auto campaigns as a beginner move. Something you graduate from once you "know what you're doing."

That's exactly backwards.

An Auto campaign is not an advertising tool. It is a data collection tool — and it happens to run ads while collecting that data.

Amazon's algorithm reads your listing and matches it against real search queries from real buyers. Not estimated search volume from a third-party tool. Not historical data.

Actual live searches from buyers actively looking for products in your category — right now.

No keyword research software in the world has access to that data. Amazon does. And the Auto campaign is your direct connection to it.

Why sellers get this wrong.

Auto campaigns look messy in the early weeks. You pull the Search Term Report and see dozens of irrelevant matches. Weird long-tail phrases. Searches that make no sense for your listing.

Most sellers conclude the campaign isn't working and pause it — or ignore the report entirely.

What they're missing is buried inside that noise:

→ Long-tail terms with low competition and high purchase intent no tool would suggest
→ Seasonal trends that emerge weeks before keyword tools pick them up
→ Competitor brand terms your buyers use as category navigation
→ Exact buyer phrasing — often different from how you'd describe your own product

The right way to run it.

Step 1 — Set conservative bids and let it run Optimise for data, not profit. Run for at least 2 weeks before drawing conclusions.

Step 2 — Pull the Search Term Report weekly Two filters: converting terms (sales at acceptable ACoS) and non-converting terms (10+ clicks, zero sales).

Step 3 — Graduate the winners Move converting terms into a Manual Exact campaign. Not guessing — scaling what's already proven.

Step 4 — Negate the losers Add non-converters as Negative Exact keywords. Permanently stop Amazon spending your budget on searches that don't buy.

Auto = the wide fishing net. Manual Exact = the spear.

You don't throw the spear until you know exactly where the fish are.

The sellers with the lowest wasted spend aren't the ones with the best tools.

They're the ones reading what Amazon is already telling them — through a campaign most sellers underestimate, misuse, or turn off too early.

posts.text:
Most Amazon sellers think more ad spend means more sales.


It doesn't.

I've seen sellers double their daily budget and watch their ACOS get worse.

I've seen sellers cut their budget by 40% and increase their revenue.

Here's why more spend without the right foundation is losing money faster — and what actually drives profitable growth on Amazon PPC.

The real relationship between ad spend and performance.
Amazon's algorithm doesn't reward the highest spender.

It rewards the strongest buying signals — clicks that convert, sessions that purchase, listings that satisfy intent.

More budget on a weak campaign doesn't bring more sales. It brings more impressions on the same underperforming keywords.

More spend on a broken campaign = faster drain, same poor results.
The metric sellers misread most.

Daily budget is not your growth lever. It's your ceiling.

Your real growth lever is your bid efficiency — how much you're paying per click relative to the value of each conversion.


Two sellers. Same $100/day budget:

Seller A — Broad match campaigns, unstructured keywords, no negatives.
Average CPC: $1.20 | CVR: 8% | Cost per sale: $15.00

Seller B — Structured campaigns, exact match targeting, regular negative keyword reviews.
Average CPC: $0.80 | CVR: 14% | Cost per sale: $5.71

Seller A is spending the same money and getting one sale for every $15 spent.

Seller B is getting one sale for every $5.71 spent.
Same budget. Seller B generates 2.6x more sales.

The difference has nothing to do with how much they're spending. It has everything to do with how they're spending it.

What actually moves the needle.

Before increasing budget on any Amazon campaign, audit these three things first:

Your Click-Through Rate (CTR)

If your CTR is below 0.3%, buyers are seeing your ad and choosing not to click. More budget just means more people ignoring your listing. The fix is your main image and title — not your spend.

Your Conversion Rate (CVR)

If CVR is below 10%, traffic is landing on your listing and leaving without buying. More budget sends more people to a listing that doesn't convert. The fix is your bullet points, A+ content, pricing, and reviews — not your spend.

Your Search Term Relevance

Pull your Search Term Report. If more than 20% of your spend is going to irrelevant or non-converting terms, increasing budget multiplies that waste. The fix is negative keywords and tighter match types — not more spend.

Only when CTR is healthy, CVR is above 10%, and your search terms are relevant — should you increase your daily budget.

At that point, scaling spend is simply pouring fuel on a fire that's already burning cleanly.

The principle.

Spend efficiency compounds.

A campaign with strong bid efficiency, clean targeting, and a converting listing will generate better results at $50/day than a poorly structured campaign at $200/day.

Fix the structure first.

Fix the listing second.

Scale the spend third.

In that order. Never the reverse.

99% of Amazon sellers running ads have the wrong campaign structure.


Not the wrong keywords. Not the wrong bids.

The wrong foundation — and it's costing them thousands in wasted spend every month.

Here's the 3-campaign structure every Amazon brand needs 👇

Most sellers open Seller Central, create one Sponsored Products campaign, dump 50 keywords in, set a $50/day budget and wonder why nothing works.

The problem isn't the keywords. It's that one campaign can't do three different jobs at the same time.

Discovery, control, and defence are three separate functions. They need three separate campaigns.

Campaign 1: The Discovery Campaign (Auto)

This is your research engine.

An Auto campaign lets Amazon match your listing to search terms algorithmically. You're not in control — and that's the point.

Auto campaigns surface terms you'd never think to target manually. Some will be irrelevant. Some will be goldmines.

How to run it properly: 

→ Start with conservative bids for your category 
→ Run for at least 2 weeks before drawing conclusions 
→ Pull your Search Term Report weekly
→ Identifying converting terms — those graduate to your Manual campaign

The Auto campaign is not where you make money. It's where you find the terms that will.

Campaign 2: The Control Campaign (Manual Exact)

This is your profit engine.

Move winning search terms from Auto into a Manual Exact campaign. Now you control exactly what triggers your ad — no algorithm guesswork.

Why Exact match?
→ Precise data — you know exactly which term is converting
→ Precise bidding — raise or lower bids based on actual performance
→ No bleed — irrelevant keyword variations won't drain your budget

Rule of thumb: 10+ clicks with no sale → add as Negative in both campaigns. 

Generates a sale → graduate to Manual Exact.

Campaign 3: The Defence Campaign (Competitor ASIN Targeting)

This is your moat.

Targeting competitor ASINs via Sponsored Products or Sponsored Display puts your listing directly on their product pages — intercepting buyers already in purchase mode.

→ Your competitor is paying to rank — you're harvesting that traffic
→ It's the highest-intent audience on the platform outside branded search

Start with the top 5–10 ASINs in your niche. If your listing doesn't convert against competitor traffic, the problem is your listing — not the campaign.

Auto feeds Manual. Manual generates data. Competitor targeting compounds it.
Each campaign has one job. One budget. One optimisation goal.

Metrics to track:

→ Auto: Search Term Report, keyword discovery rate
→ Manual Exact: ACOS, CVR, Impression Share
→ Competitor ASIN: CTR, CVR, ACOS vs. category average

Structure is clarity. Clarity is control. Control is profit.

posts.text:
Most Amazon sellers are waiting for reviews before they advertise.



Here's why that logic is costing them their ranking window.

The misconception:

Reviews build rankings.

The reality:

Rankings build reviews.
Amazon's algorithm doesn't rank products because they have reviews. It ranks products that demonstrate buying signals — clicks, conversions, and session velocity. Reviews are simply a byproduct of that process.

Here's how the algorithm actually works on a new listing:

When Amazon indexes a new ASIN, there's a short window — typically the first 2 weeks — where the algorithm is actively collecting data to decide where to rank you.

During this window, it's watching for 3 signals:

-- Click-Through Rate
Are people clicking your listing when they see it in search results? If your main image isn't compelling enough to earn the click, no amount of ad spend will save you.

-- Conversion Rate

Of the people who land on your listing, how many are buying? Amazon considers 10%+ a healthy baseline. Below that, the algorithm treats your listing as a mismatch for the keyword.

-- Session Velocity

How many unique visitors is your listing getting — and how consistently? Sporadic traffic sends weak signals. Steady, daily traffic tells the algorithm your listing is relevant.

What most sellers get wrong:

They wait 30–60 days building reviews through Vine or follow-up emails before running any ads.

By then, the indexing window has closed. The algorithm has already deprioritised the listing. They're now fighting uphill against competitors who moved faster.

What actually works:

Before running ads, the listing needs to be conversion-ready — not just keyword-rich. That means:

→ Main image optimised for CTR over aesthetics
→ Bullet points written around objections, not features
→ A+ content that builds enough trust to convert cold traffic

Once the listing converts, then you send targeted traffic — not broad keywords, but competitor ASINs where buyers already have high purchase intent.

The goal is to generate clean buying signals during that indexing window.
Reviews follow naturally once the listing is ranking and getting organic traffic.

The takeaway:

A new Amazon listing doesn't need reviews to rank.
It needs signals — and signals come from a listing that converts, not one that waits.

posts.text:
From $14k → $53k in 30 days: the exact sequence



A new seller came in doing ~$14k/month. Campaigns were almost all Auto, budgets were scattered, and branded queries weren’t protected. Inventory was tight and demand was uneven.

The ask: reach $100k/month as inventory lands in FBA.

What we changed (no fluff, just sequence):

Retail readiness audit — confirmed Buy Box stability, pricing, and listings to avoid wasting PPC spend.
Rebuilt structure — split into Exact / Phrase / Broad (with modifiers) for clean intent layers.
Brand defense — captured branded keywords and added ASIN shielding to prevent leakage.
Search-term mining + negatives — harvested winners; blocked low-intent terms to cut bleed.
Performance tiers (A/B/C) — bids and budgets aligned to CVR and contribution; capped CPC on marginal queries.
Placement + dayparting — adjusted Top-of-Search multipliers and scheduled around conversion windows.
Weekly reallocation — moved budget toward proven targets; tracked TACoS/ACOS and CPC trend, not vanity metrics.
Result: $53k in 30 days (+279% MoM).
 Next milestone: $100k as FBA stock arrives and exact-match winners scale.

Why it worked:

Structure > tactics. Clean match-type lanes made attribution clear.
Defense first. Owning branded terms reduced blended acquisition cost (TACoS).
Negatives every week. Spend concentrated on queries that converted.
Budget follows proof. We funded what worked and cut what didn’t—quickly.
Inventory and ads moved together. Client shipped to FBA to sustain the curve.

If you manage Amazon PPC and growth stalls, use this checklist:

Protect brand terms before chasing category terms.
Separate Exact / Phrase / Broad to control intent and bids.
Mine search terms twice per week; add negatives the same day.
Tier campaigns by performance; cap CPCs where CVR is volatile.
Tune placement multipliers and dayparting to match conversion hours.
Track TACoS weekly; reallocate budget, don’t “set and forget.”

Goal: a durable path to $100k/month without gimmicks—just disciplined Amazon Advertising (Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Sponsored Display), clean measurement, and inventory alignment.

Optimizing Your Amazon Advertising: Tackling Keyword Cannibalization



Keyword cannibalization in Amazon PPC is a challenge every seller should tackle head-on. 

It occurs when multiple campaigns or ad groups inadvertently compete for the same keywords, negatively impacting campaign performance.


Causes of Keyword Cannibalization:
Poor campaign structure
Overlapping keyword targeting
Overlapping match types 
Keyword duplications

Effects of Keyword Cannibalization:
Fluctuation in Click Through Rate (CTR) 
High Cost per Click (CPC)
In-effective Ads Spend
Low Conversion (CVR) 
Poor Ads Efficency

Solution of Keyword Cannibalization:
Right campaign Nomenclature
